def check_r_package(pkg):
    "Tests whether the R package *pkg* is installed."
    r_path = get_r_path()
    if r_path is None:
        # Rscript is not installed, so no R package can be available
        return False
    cmd = [r_path, "-e", f"library({pkg})"]
    logger.debug("check_r_package cmd: %s", cmd)
    p = subprocess.run(cmd, shell=False, capture_output=True)
    logger.debug("check_r_package stdout:\n%s", pformat(p.stdout.decode("utf-8")))
    logger.debug("check_r_package stderr:\n%s", pformat(p.stderr.decode("utf-8")))

    return p.returncode == 0

docs.title: Concepts & file formats
docs.text:
detk is built around two file types that every tool shares: the counts matrix file and the column data file (also called the metadata or covariates file). Both are plain character-delimited text; detk sniffs the delimiter on input, and always writes comma-separated output.

The delimiter is sniffed from the first line (comma, tab, semicolon, pipe, then space). A first line with none of them is a one-field header, as R's write.table writes over row names ("condition" over "S1","a"); then the delimiter is sniffed from the first data lines, which must all split on it into the same number of fields. A one-field header over rows that split unalike (condition over S1,a and S2) is an error, naming the file, the delimiter and the first two lines whose field counts differ: quote a field that holds the delimiter, or give every line the same fields. When no data line has a delimiter either, the file is read as one column, such as a list of IDs.

docs.title: The counts matrix file
docs.text:
Every tool accepts a counts matrix of the form:

gene_id sample_1 sample_2 ... sample_m gene_1 10000 1244 ... 2935 gene_2 2023 1534 ... 1308 gene_3 5 2 ... 19 ... ... ... ... ... gene_n 5 2 ... 150031
  • The first column must contain unique gene or feature identifiers — Ensembl gene IDs, miRBase IDs, ChIP-seq peaks, genomic bins, anything.
  • The remaining column names must be unique sample identifiers.
  • The name of the first column doesn't matter; every row must have the same number of fields.

detk-norm, detk-de, detk-transform, detk-stats, detk-filter, detk-outlier, detk-util tidy, tidy-counts and tidy-covs and detk-wrapr run check a counts matrix as read, before the column data selects or reorders any sample, and exit 1 (a bad input file, see Exit codes) naming the first offender and how many more there are (DETK-0601, DETK-0830, DETK-0850).

  • in each of those commands: a sample named more than once in the header, and a feature ID listed more than once. Positions are counted in the file, from 1, among the samples and the features.
  • in the commands that need raw counts: also a negative count, a sample with no numeric value, and a sample whose counts sum to 0 (zero depth).
Needs raw counts (all five checks) May take a normalized or transformed matrix (repeated IDs only) detk-norm deseq2, library, cpm, fpkm, tpm detk-de firth detk-de deseq2 detk-transform plog detk-transform vst, rlog detk-stats (every subcommand) detk-filter detk-outlier entropy, shrink detk-util tidy, tidy-counts, tidy-covs detk-wrapr run

A normalized or log-transformed matrix may hold negative values or a column of zeros, so the commands on the right accept them. The commands on the left model or scale counts, which a negative value or an empty sample would make wrong without a word.

docs.title: The column data file
docs.text:
Tools that need per-sample information (differential expression, PCA coloring, group-wise filtering) take a column data file:

sample_names condition sex ... covariate_p sample_1 case M ... c1 sample_2 control F ... c9 ... ... ... ... ... sample_m case F ... c3

The first column holds sample names matching the column names of the counts file; remaining columns hold any covariates needed for analysis. The two files must name the same samples: a sample in only one of them is an error (exit 1) that names it, rather than a silent subset (DETK-0600). detk matches the samples up by name, so the column data rows may come in any order, but it is good practice to keep the order consistent — tools accept a --strict flag to require it. To analyse only some of the samples, subset the files explicitly with the detk-util tidy commands, which keep the samples in both and reorder the column data to the counts.

docs.title: Design formulas
docs.text: Tools that fit models (detk-de, non-blind detk-transform rlog) take a design formula written in detk's formula mini-language, which resolves column data columns into a full-rank model matrix with machine-friendly column names like Status__case.

docs.title: The report layer
docs.text: Every tool invocation (unless --no-report is passed) drops a JSON document describing its parameters and results into detk_report/json/. The detk-report tool renders all accumulated documents into a single self-contained HTML report. The JSON documents are stable, machine-readable provenance — you can consume them directly in downstream tooling.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Every detk command exits with one of three codes (DETK-0031), which its --help also states:

Code Meaning 0 success (and --help, --version) 2 usage error: the command line is wrong, such as an unknown option, a missing argument, a bad option value or an invalid design formula; the usage is printed with the error 1 any other failure: a bad input file, a missing R or R package, a step that fails

A failure prints one line on stderr, <command>: error: <cause>; with --verbose the traceback is printed before it. A script can tell a mistake in its own command line (2) from a problem with the data or the environment (1).

docs.title: Shell completion
docs.text:
detk ships completion scripts for bash, zsh and tcsh (DETK-0032), which complete every detk command (detk and each detk-<command>), its subcommands, options and choices, and file names where an argument takes a file. detk completion <shell> prints the script; load it from your shell's startup file:

# bash, in ~/.bashrc
eval "$(detk completion bash)"

# zsh, in ~/.zshrc, after compinit
eval "$(detk completion zsh)"

# tcsh: write the script once, then source it in ~/.tcshrc
detk completion tcsh > ~/.detk.tcsh
source ~/.detk.tcsh

The scripts are part of the installed package, so printing one needs nothing else installed. Open a new shell (or source the startup file) for the completion to take effect.

docs.title: Worked example: the airway dataset
docs.text:
detk's example report is a complete differential expression analysis of a real, public RNA-seq dataset, airway (GEO GSE52778): human airway smooth muscle cells from four donor cell lines, treated with dexamethasone or untreated, 8 samples and 63,677 Ensembl genes, from the airway Bioconductor data package (Himes et al. 2014, PMID 24926665).

Open the finished example report: one self-contained HTML file, everything client-side, nothing leaves your browser.

The run's machine-readable provenance is published alongside it: ro-crate-metadata.json, a Process Run Crate describing every step of the run.

docs.title: How it was made
docs.text: The tutorial Differential expression on airway is the whole analysis, step by step, with the output to expect at each one: getting the data, summary statistics, filtering, DESeq2 normalization, the variance-stabilizing transform, entropy outliers, detk-de deseq2 with the cell line as a covariate, gene symbols, and the report and the crate. detk's tests run that page, and the report above is the one its run made (examples/airway/run.sh in the repository runs the page and publishes the report here).

docs.title: Using a workflow manager
docs.text: Each step is a plain command-line filter, so the pipeline drops directly into Snakemake, Nextflow, or a shell script — see the Quickstart for a Snakemake version of this same shape.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Some of the important operations in detk, most notably the de module, require the user to specify a statistical model. General-purpose formula libraries such as R's model.matrix and the Python package formulaic describe statistical models in just this way, but their syntax is not very machine-readable. A linear model relating a continuous quantity to a categorical variable looks like:

cont_var ~ C(cat_var, levels=['A','B','C'])

and the resulting design matrix has columns named something like:

cont_var ~ Intercept + C(cat_var, levels=['A','B','C'])[T.B] + C(cat_var, levels=['A','B','C'])[T.C]

This is at least a little bit yuck, and gets very yuck as the number of variables grows. detk therefore implements its own formula syntax, the detk formula syntax, where the same model is written:

cont_var ~ cat_var[A,B,C]

producing the full matrix:

cont_var ~ Intercept + cat_var__B + cat_var__C

These column names are much more amenable to programmatic use. detk translates the formula for formulaic, which resolves the full-rank model matrix from the column data.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Formula terms refer to column names of the column data file. The examples below use this column data:

cont binary_str binary_int cat_str cat_int flag 0.13 case 1 A 1 TRUE 0.97 control 0 B 2 FALSE 0.22 case 1 A 1 TRUE 0.76 control 0 C 3 FALSE 0.69 control 0 C 3 TRUE 0.08 case 1 A 1 FALSE 0.17 case 1 B 2 TRUE 0.53 control 0 C 3 FALSE

There are four types of terms:

  • scalar — variables treated as purely numeric: continuous measures and ordinal variables, e.g. cont, binary_int, or cat_int.
  • binary — two-level categories encoded as strings, written binary_str or, with an explicit reference group, binary_str[control]. Binary variables use a dummy encoding: a single binary vector in the full model matrix. A column of TRUE/FALSE values is binary too: flag gives flag__True, with FALSE the reference, and flag[TRUE] gives flag__False.
  • multinomial — categorical variables with more than two levels, written cat_str or cat_str[A,B,C,D] to specify the level order. The first level (or alphabetically first if omitted) is the reference group. Dummy encoding produces one binary vector per non-reference level.
  • interactions — binary_str:cat_str is the interaction of two terms, and binary_str*cat_str is short for binary_str + cat_str + binary_str:cat_str. Either side of : or * may be any term above, with a reference or level list (binary_str[control]:cat_str).

Formulas take column names only. A term that is not a column and looks like a function call, such as np.log(cont) or log2(cont), is an error: a derived column, such as a log-transformed covariate, belongs in the column data file, where the formula can name it. A column whose name really is such a string, say log2(cont), is still a column.

Derived covariates with Miller gives tested recipes for the usual derived columns (a log, a log with a pseudocount, a z-score, centring, min-max and a constant column), each with the checks that stop it on a missing value or a log of zero, and each recorded with detk-util record so the step shows in the report and the provenance.

Column names in a formula start with a letter or underscore. A term that looks like a number, such as 3, 2.5 or -2.5, is an error on either side of ~, whether or not the column data has a column by that name: a number is never a column name. Only 0 and 1 have a meaning, the intercept: counts ~ 0 + cont and counts ~ cont - 1 leave it out, counts ~ 1 is the intercept alone. A column whose name looks like a number, a time point or a dose written as a header, has to be renamed in the column data file before a formula can name it; the error message says so (DETK-0190).

An error in a formula is reported in one line naming the offending term: a term that is not a column of the column data file (with the columns it has), a reference level its column does not have (with the values it has), or a part of the formula detk cannot read.

Every model has a left hand side and a right hand side separated by ~. In general there should be a single term on the left hand side.

Output column names in the full model matrix follow three patterns:

  • literal pass-through — exactly the column name (scalar terms)
  • categorical — <variable name>__<level>
  • interaction — the columns of each term joined by :, e.g. binary_str__control:cat_str__B

The double underscore makes it easy to recognize which variable an output column refers to, and makes downstream programmatic analysis easier.

The columns come in a fixed order: the Intercept, then the columns of the single terms in the order they are written, then the interactions. For example, cont ~ binary_str*cat_str gives:

cont ~ Intercept + binary_str__control + cat_str__B + cat_str__C +
    binary_str__control:cat_str__B + binary_str__control:cat_str__C

An interaction written alone is coded full rank, which brings in main-effect columns of one of its terms. cont ~ binary_str:cat_str gives:

cont ~ Intercept + cat_str__B + cat_str__C + binary_str__control:cat_str__A +
    binary_str__control:cat_str__B + binary_str__control:cat_str__C

Some mostly non-differential-expression examples:

height ~ weight + age
disease_status[control] ~ age_at_death + batch[1] + counts
gross_domestic_product ~ continent[NoAm] + population + election_year[no]

giving full model matrix columns like the ones below. batch holds the integers 1, 2 and 3, so batch alone would be a scalar term; batch[1] makes it categorical with 1 the reference. The levels of a category without a level list come in sorted order.

height ~ Intercept + weight + age
disease_status__case ~ Intercept + age_at_death + batch__2 + batch__3 + counts
gross_domestic_product ~ Intercept + continent__Asia + continent__Aust +
    continent__Euro + continent__SoAm + continent__SoPo + population +
    election_year__yes

docs.title: The special counts term
docs.text:
For detk tools that fit a model per feature, the feature counts must appear somewhere in the model. Since formula terms refer to column data columns, detk provides the special term counts for this purpose; include it as if it were a normal scalar variable.

Where counts goes depends on the DE method:

  • DESeq2: counts must be the only term on the left hand side — counts ~ AgeOfDeath + Status
  • Firth logistic regression: counts goes on the right hand side, with the sample class on the left — Status ~ AgeOfDeath + counts

detk checks that the design has counts where the method expects it.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
detk implements the common operations when working with count matrices from high-throughput sequencing experiments. The following diagram illustrates a simple RNA-seq workflow downstream of quantification:

This workflow performs the following, all without any custom code:

  1. Takes the output from read counting (e.g. htseq-count) or expression estimation software (e.g. salmon or kallisto) and combines them into a single counts matrix with detk-util gather
  2. Calculates statistics on the zero-ness of genes to guide feature filtering with detk-stats rowzero
  3. Keeps the rows with more than half of their counts nonzero with detk-filter
  4. Normalizes the filtered matrix with the DESeq2 procedure via detk-norm deseq2
  5. Computes principal components on the normalized matrix to identify outlier samples with detk-stats pca
  6. Removes a hypothetical outlier sample with csvcut from csvkit
  7. Runs DESeq2 differential expression with detk-de deseq2
  8. Computes pre-ranked GSEA on the DE statistics with detk-enrich fgsea

On the command line, the core of that workflow is below, for a counts matrix raw_counts.csv, a column data file sample_info.csv whose cond column says which samples are control and which treated, and the gene sets of msigdb_c2cp.gmt. The DESeq2 result names each column by its model term, so the treated-versus-control log fold change, the statistic GSEA ranks by, is cond__treated__log2FoldChange:

detk-stats rowzero -o raw_counts_rowzero_stats.csv raw_counts.csv
detk-filter "nonzero(all) > 0.5" -o raw_counts_filtered.csv raw_counts.csv
detk-norm deseq2 -o norm_counts_filtered.csv raw_counts_filtered.csv
detk-stats pca -o norm_counts_filtered_pca.csv norm_counts_filtered.csv
detk-de deseq2 -o deseq2_results.csv "counts ~ cond[control]" raw_counts_filtered.csv sample_info.csv
detk-enrich fgsea -o gsea_results.csv -i gene -c cond__treated__log2FoldChange msigdb_c2cp.gmt deseq2_results.csv
detk-report generate

detk-de deseq2 does not give the same padj as a default DESeq2 vignette run (DESeq(dds) then results(dds)). It reports the Wald test of every coefficient in the model, and its padj is the Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment over all genes: no independent filtering is performed, and there is no Cook's distance cutoff, so no p-value is set to NA as an outlier. The detk-de deseq2 page states the results() settings this matches and the other ways it differs from the default analysis.

The final command renders every step's recorded JSON into a single self-contained HTML report.

docs.title: Using a workflow manager
docs.text:
detk tools are plain command-line filters, which makes them trivial to embed in whichever workflow manager you already use. The same workflow in Snakemake:

from glob import glob

rule all:
    input:
        'detk_report/detk_report.html',
        'msigdb_c2cp_gsea_results.csv'

rule gather_counts:
    input: glob('sample_*__salmon_counts/quant.sf')
    output: 'raw_counts.csv'
    shell:
        '''
        detk-util gather --name-from="([^/]+)__salmon_counts/" \
            -o {output} {input}
        '''

rule raw_rowzero:
    input: 'raw_counts.csv'
    output: 'raw_counts_rowzero_stats.csv'
    shell:
        'detk-stats rowzero -o {output} {input}'

rule filter_raw:
    input: 'raw_counts.csv'
    output: 'raw_counts_filtered.csv'
    shell:
        'detk-filter "nonzero(all) > 0.5" -o {output} {input}'

rule deseq2_norm:
    input: 'raw_counts_filtered.csv'
    output: 'norm_counts_filtered.csv'
    shell:
        'detk-norm deseq2 -o {output} {input}'

rule pca:
    input: 'norm_counts_filtered.csv'
    output: 'norm_counts_filtered_pca.csv'
    shell:
        'detk-stats pca -o {output} {input}'

rule de:
    input:
        counts='raw_counts_filtered.csv',
        covs='sample_info.csv'
    output: 'deseq2_results.csv'
    shell:
        'detk-de deseq2 -o {output} "counts ~ cond[control]" {input.counts} {input.covs}'

rule gsea:
    input:
        de='deseq2_results.csv',
        gmt='msigdb_c2cp.gmt'
    output: 'msigdb_c2cp_gsea_results.csv'
    shell:
        'detk-enrich fgsea -o {output} -i gene -c cond__treated__log2FoldChange {input.gmt} {input.de}'

rule generate_detk_report:
    input:
        rules.raw_rowzero.output,
        rules.pca.output,
        rules.de.output
    output: 'detk_report/detk_report.html'
    shell:
        'detk-report generate'

Run with snakemake --cores 1. A Nextflow process wrapping any of these commands looks the same: detk needs nothing from the workflow manager beyond a shell.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
detk's reporting layer gives every analysis two artifacts for free:

  1. Machine-readable provenance — every tool invocation records a JSON document capturing what was run, with what parameters, and what it found.
  2. A human-readable report — a single, self-contained HTML file rendering all recorded results as interactive charts. No network access, no external files; you can email it, archive it, or attach it to a paper.

See one now: a live example report generated from the public airway RNA-seq dataset by the worked example.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Unless --no-report is passed, each detk tool serializes a JSON document into <report-dir>/json/ (default ./detk_report/json/) as a side effect of the run. Documents are named by a content hash of what identifies a run (see What identifies a record), so re-running the same command updates its document in place rather than accumulating duplicates, while runs with different parameters or different files coexist.

Run tools, then render:

detk-stats summary raw_counts.csv sample_info.csv -o raw_stats.csv
detk-filter "nonzero(all) > 0.5" -o filtered.csv raw_counts.csv
detk-norm deseq2 -o norm.csv filtered.csv

detk-report generate

This produces detk_report/detk_report.html containing a view for every recorded module, organized by family (stats, filter, norm, ...) in a collapsible navigation tray.

usage: detk-report generate [options]

options:
  -h, --help  Print this help and exit
  --dev       Pretty-print the embedded JSON payload (larger file, easier to
              read)

detk-report generate reads the report directory given with --report-dir (default ./detk_report), one of the common options.

detk-report clean deletes the report directory, with its accumulated JSON, the HTML report and the provenance crate in it.

usage: detk-report clean [options]

options:
  -h, --help  Print this help and exit

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
• Charts are rendered with Vega-Lite (vendored into the HTML — the report works offline forever).
  • Light/dark theme toggle, persisted across visits.
  • Every chart offers SVG/PNG export for figures, and a "Show data" toggle revealing the exact JSON the chart was built from — the report never shows you a picture you can't trace back to data.
  • Modules without a dedicated chart yet render their raw JSON rather than being dropped.

docs.title: The module JSON documents
docs.text:
Each document contains the module's name, the params it was invoked with, its report-relevant properties, the detk version, timing, the process argument vector, and input/output file paths. The document format is versioned (schema_version) and specified by a JSON Schema shipped inside the package (de_toolkit/module_schema.json); every emitted document is validated against it in detk's test suite. For example (abbreviated):

{
  "name": "colzero",
  "detk_version": "1.0.0",
  "params": {},
  "properties": {
    "zeros": [
      {"name": "sample_1", "zero_count": 4102, "zero_frac": 0.15, "...": "..."}
    ]
  },
  "in_file_path": "raw_counts.csv",
  "out_file_path": "raw_stats.csv"
}

docs.title: What identifies a record
docs.text:
A document's id, and so its file name json/<id>.json, is a hash of:

  • the module name and its params
  • every input and output path, as recorded (relative to workdir): in_file_path, out_file_path, column_data_path and, when present, in_file_paths and out_file_paths
  • the recorded command line, argv
  • the detk version

Two runs that differ in any of these keep two records: detk-filter run with -o a.csv and then -o b.csv, detk-de deseq2 run on two sample information files, or detk-enrich fgsea run on two results files (fgsea records its GMT as in_file_path and both the GMT and the results file in in_file_paths). A run identical in all of them, the same command from the same directory, writes the same id and replaces its one record. Because paths and the command line are hashed as recorded, an absolute path and its relative spelling give the same id; a command spelled differently (-o for --output, or an extra -v) gives a new one. Ids change with each detk version.

docs.title: Document schema
docs.text:
The envelope is versioned (schema_version, currently 1.2) and specified by a JSON Schema shipped inside the package at de_toolkit/module_schema.json (view on GitHub). Required fields:

Field Type Meaning name string module name (lowercased DetkModule subclass) id string content hash of what identifies the run (name, params, every input and output path, command line, detk version); see What identifies a record schema_version string version of this envelope format detk_version string de_toolkit version that wrote the document last_modified integer unix ms timestamp of the write params object invocation parameters (empty only for modules that take none) properties object module-specific results consumed by the report views

Optional fields:

Field Type Meaning start_time / end_time string ISO 8601 UTC argv array the command line; argv[0] is the command's name only (detk-stats); the other arguments as typed, except that an absolute path, alone or as an option's value (--report-dir=/abs/rep, -o/abs/out.csv), is written relative to workdir, so the line re-runs the same from there workdir string the directory the command ran in, relative to the report directory: .. for the default ./detk_report in_file_path, out_file_path, column_data_path string the input, output and column data files, relative to workdir (a path typed as absolute is written relative too) in_file_paths, out_file_paths array since 1.1: every input and output file of a step with several, each relative to workdir; written by detk-util record and by each command that reads or writes a file besides its primary input and output (annotate's mapping file, gather's per-sample files, fgsea's results file, the fpkm and tpm lengths file, a --size-factors, --rda or --plot-output file), and left out otherwise; their first entries are also in_file_path and out_file_path

So a file's location is the report directory, then workdir, then the path: detk_report/../counts.csv. No recorded path is absolute, whether you typed paths relative or absolute: argv and the parameters and checksums of detk-util record are written relative to workdir too (DETK-0281), so a report directory can be moved or published as it is. What that leaves out:

  • An argument that is not a path. detk rewrites an argument that is an absolute path (or an option's value that is one), not paths inside an argument. An argument counts as a path when it is an absolute path that exists, whitespace or not (/home/me/proj/My Data/c.csv is written My Data/c.csv, DETK-0590); one that does not exist counts only when it starts with /, has no whitespace and its parent directory exists (DETK-0580), as an output not yet written does. Any other argument is written as typed, even one that starts with /: an awk program ('/^gene/ {print}'), a regular expression ('/^g1,/') or a shell script (sh -c "/usr/bin/env echo hi"). An absolute path to a file in a directory that does not exist is kept as typed too. The script of sh -c is one argument, so it is written as typed, absolute paths and all. Run in /home/me/proj,

    $ detk-util record -i /home/me/proj/a.csv -o /home/me/proj/b.csv -- sh -c "cp /home/me/proj/a.csv /home/me/proj/b.csv"

    records

    {
  "argv": ["detk-util", "record", "-i", "a.csv", "-o", "b.csv", "--",
           "sh", "-c", "cp /home/me/proj/a.csv /home/me/proj/b.csv"],
  "in_file_paths": ["a.csv"],
  "out_file_paths": ["b.csv"]
}

    so write such steps with relative paths (sh -c "cp a.csv b.csv"). - The program of a recorded step. Typed as an absolute path, it is written by its name when PATH finds that same file by that name (DETK-0390): detk-util record ... -- /usr/bin/cp a.csv b.csv records cp a.csv b.csv, as a detk command's argv[0] is its name. A program PATH does not find, or finds as another file, is written relative like any other path. So on a system where /bin and /usr/bin are separate directories, /bin/cp is recorded as a relative path (../../../bin/cp from /home/me/proj) when PATH finds /usr/bin/cp first; where /bin is a link to /usr/bin, as on most current Linux systems, it is the same file and is written cp. Type the program by its name to record it by its name. - The directories a relative path climbs through. With the report directory, or a file, in another tree from the working directory, the ../ chain spells that tree's directories: --report-dir /tmp/rep run in /home/me/proj records workdir as ../../home/me/proj. That is the only form of workdir that keeps the location rule above, so detk keeps it; keep the report directory and the data under the working directory to avoid it.

Since 1.2; documents of 1.0 and 1.1 hold workdir and argv[0] absolute, and an absolute workdir joined to the report directory is itself, so the same rule reads them.

The version is major.minor: the minor version goes up for an addition every older document still satisfies, or a change of what a field holds that the same rule still reads in older documents (1.1 added the two optional lists; 1.2 made the paths relative), the major version for a change that is not. Every document detk emits is validated against the schema in the test suite; validate your own consumers against the same file. Small p-values never appear as raw floats in properties — the encoder rounds floats to 3 decimals, so modules emit -log10 values or preformatted strings instead.

These documents are the intended integration point for any downstream tooling that wants to consume detk results programmatically — LIMS systems, QC dashboards, meta-analyses. The same JSON is also embedded verbatim inside the generated HTML, so a report file is self-certifying: the data behind every chart travels with it.

docs.title: Standards-based provenance: the Process Run Crate
docs.text:
Alongside the report, in the report directory, detk writes an ro-crate-metadata.json, describing every recorded invocation in community-standard terms: the Process Run Crate profile of Workflow Run RO-Crate, built on RO-Crate. This is a second, standards-facing view of the same facts as the module JSON:

  • each detk invocation is a CreateAction, with start/end times
  • each subtool (e.g. detk-norm deseq2) is a SoftwareApplication with its version
  • invocation parameters are PropertyValue entities
  • input and output files are shared File entities, so the chaining of tools through files — the implicit workflow — is visible in the metadata graph
  • standard output is not listed as a file: a command that wrote its result to stdout (out_file_path stdout, the -o default) has no File for it. A file really named stdout is recorded ./stdout and listed
  • a step recorded by detk-util record is a CreateAction whose instrument is the external tool, with its version, and lists every file it was given with -i and -o
  • only the files detk-util record checksummed carry sha256 and contentSize: the inputs and outputs of a step it recorded. The files of detk commands carry neither, unless a recorded step also read or wrote the same file

The crate is rooted in the report directory, so each report directory has its own crate: two analyses run in one directory with different --report-dir values never overwrite each other's provenance. Every file is named by its path relative to the report directory (../counts.csv for a file in the working directory of the default ./detk_report), never by an absolute path or file:// URI, so the report directory is a self-describing research object wherever it is copied, as long as the files beside it come too. Standard RO-Crate tooling (rocrate-validator, runcrate report, WorkflowHub, Zenodo RO-Crate deposits) can inspect it without detk installed, and the crate maps to W3C PROV-O via the profile's published mapping. detk validates its emitted crates against the Process Run Crate profile in its test suite, and checks that the crate of a filter -> DESeq2 -> fgsea chain traces the enrichment table, from each file to the action whose result it is and on to that action's inputs, back to the counts and the sample information file.

The crate is derived entirely from the module JSON under <report-dir>/json/, is rewritten on every report generation, and is removed with the report directory by detk-report clean. (detk before 1.0 wrote it to the working directory; clean leaves such a ./ro-crate-metadata.json alone.) detk does not assert a license over your data — the crate's license field says so explicitly; replace it with your license when publishing.

Archiving: if you publish the analysis directory to Zenodo/OSF (e.g. with a sync tool such as datapin), the report directory in the deposit is a valid RO-Crate whose references reach the data beside it, so the archived object remains machine-readable provenance, not just a pile of CSVs.

docs.title: Using reports in a workflow
docs.text: Report JSON accumulates in the working directory (or wherever --report-dir points), so the natural pattern in a workflow manager is to make detk-report generate a final step that depends on all detk-invoking steps — see the Quickstart for a complete Snakemake example.

docs.title: Library usage
docs.text:
From Python, modules emit their JSON through a context manager:

from de_toolkit.report import DetkReport
from de_toolkit.stats import BaseStats
from de_toolkit.common import CountMatrixFile

with open("counts.csv") as f:
    counts = CountMatrixFile(f)

with DetkReport("my_report_dir") as r:
    r.add_module(
        BaseStats(counts),
        in_file_path="counts.csv",
        workdir=".",
    )
# my_report_dir/detk_report.html is written on context exit

docs.title: Derived covariates with Miller
docs.text:
A design formula takes column names only: detk does not compute log2(conc) or a z-score of age inside a formula. A derived covariate belongs in the column data file, as a column of its own that the formula names. This page gives a recipe for each derived column a design usually needs, written for Miller (mlr), a command line tool for CSV and other tabular files, and shows each one run through detk-util record, so the step that made the column is part of the analysis's report and provenance.

Column Recipe Value a name you pick constant the same text in every sample <column>_log2 log base 2 log2(x) <column>_log10 log base 10 log10(x) <column>_ln natural log ln(x) <column>_log2_pc1 log base 2 with a pseudocount log2(x + 1) <column>_zscore z-score (x - mean) / sd, the sd over n - 1 <column>_center centring x - mean <column>_minmax min-max (x - min) / (max - min), from 0 to 1

The names keep the source column and add a suffix with one underscore, so they cannot be mistaken for the variable__level columns of a model matrix.

Miller is not part of detk; install it from conda-forge, Homebrew or as a single binary from its releases:

$ mamba install -c conda-forge miller      # or: brew install miller
$ mlr --version
mlr 6.22.0

The recipes need Miller 6; detk's tests run them with the version conda-forge has.

docs.title: Why the recipes check their input
docs.text:
Miller does what it is told without complaint. log(0) is -Inf, the log of a negative number is NaN, and arithmetic on an empty cell gives an empty cell, each written to the output without a word. A -Inf or an empty value in a covariate makes every model that uses it fail, or worse, quietly drop samples. So each recipe checks every sample first and computes second:

  • it keeps every record until the end of the file and notes the sample of any value it cannot use: a missing or non-numeric value, a value at or below zero for a log (after the pseudocount, for _log2_pc1), or, for the z-score and min-max, a column with the same value in every sample;
  • if any were noted, it prints them to stderr, names the samples (from the first column), and stops with exit status 1 through a Miller type assertion (asserting_null), so detk-util record fails too and records nothing;
  • otherwise it adds the new column and writes every record to the output file from inside Miller (emit > @out), not through a shell redirect, so a recipe that stops leaves no output file behind.

A sheet with a header and no samples has nothing to derive from. The z-score and min-max recipes stop on it with a message of their own (age_zscore: age has no values: the sheet has no samples); the others write no output file, so detk-util record stops on the missing output. Either way it exits 1 and records nothing.

Each recipe is a Miller program kept in a shell variable, then one detk-util record command that runs it. -s col=... names the column to derive from and -s out=... the file to write, which is also the -o of detk-util record. The program does not change, so copy it as it is and change only those two and the file names. The constant column's recipe has no col=: change its column name and value ($study = "pilot") instead.

docs.title: The sample sheet
docs.text:
A small sample sheet, with zero-padded sample names, a concentration (conc, ng/µl), a dose that is zero in the controls, and the donor's age:

cat > sample_info.csv <<'EOF'
sample,condition,conc,dose,age
007,control,52.0,0,34
008,control,118.5,0,51
009,control,87.2,0,45
010,treated,64.9,10,38
011,treated,230.1,30,62
012,treated,41.3,100,29
EOF

Miller keeps every value it does not change as it was written, so 007 stays 007 and 52.0 stays 52.0 in every output below.

The same rule makes Miller read a zero-padded whole number, such as 010 or 05, as text, not as a number, so a recipe that derives from a column holding one stops and names the sample as "missing or not a number". (A decimal such as 05.5 is read as a number.) Write the value without its leading zeros (10, 5) in the sheet and run the recipe again. Do not reach for Miller's -O flag, which reads 010 as the octal number 8. Zero-padded sample names, as here, are fine: the recipes do not compute with them.

docs.text:

detk-util record -q -i sample_info.csv -o sample_info.study.csv -- \
  mlr --icsv --ocsv put -q -s out=sample_info.study.csv '$study = "pilot"; tee > @out, $*' sample_info.csv

Log base 2 of conc, as conc_log2. Miller has no log2, so the program divides the natural log by log(2):

log2='

  end {

      asserting_null("stop");

    for (i, r in @rec) { @rec[i][@col . "_log2"] = log(r[@col]) / log(2) }

docs.title: When a check fails
docs.text:
A sheet in which sample 009 has no concentration and 011 has a concentration of 0:

cat > sample_info_bad.csv <<'EOF'
sample,condition,conc,dose,age
007,control,52.0,0,34
008,control,118.5,0,51
009,control,,0,45
010,treated,64.9,10,38
011,treated,0,30,62
012,treated,41.3,100,29
EOF

The log recipe, run on it, names both samples and stops; detk-util record then stops too, with exit status 1, and records nothing:

detk-util record -q -i sample_info_bad.csv -o sample_info_bad.conc_log2.csv -- \
  mlr --icsv --ocsv put -q -s col=conc -s out=sample_info_bad.conc_log2.csv "$log2" sample_info_bad.csv

conc_log2: conc is missing, not a number or not above 0 in 009, 011
mlr: is_null type-assertion failed at NR=6 FNR=6 FILENAME=sample_info_bad.csv
detk-util: error: command failed with exit status 1: mlr --icsv --ocsv put -q -s col=conc -s out=sample_info_bad.conc_log2.csv '...' sample_info_bad.csv (--verbose for the traceback)

The second line is Miller's, from the assertion that stops it, and the last is detk-util record's, which shows the Miller program, several lines long, as '...'. There is no output file:

ls sample_info_bad*

sample_info_bad.csv

Without the check, Miller would have written -Inf for 011 and an empty conc_log2 for 009, and exited 0.

docs.title: Z-score, centring and min-max
docs.text:
The z-score of age, as age_zscore: the age less the mean age, over the sample standard deviation, the one that divides by n - 1 (as R's sd() and scale() do, and numpy's std(ddof=1)). The program computes the mean and standard deviation itself, in two passes over the values, rather than with Miller's stddev, which is computed in one pass and can be off in the last digits; on six samples that all have the value 7.2 it gives about 1e-7 (1.07e-7 on Miller 6.22), not 0. For the same reason a column that does not vary is found by its smallest and largest values being equal:

zscore='
  @rec[NR] = $*; @ids[NR] = $[[[1]]];
  if (!is_numeric($[@col])) { @bad[NR] = $[[[1]]] }
  else { @min = min(@min, $[@col]); @max = max(@max, $[@col]) }
  end {
    if (length(@rec) == 0) {
      eprint @col . "_zscore: " . @col . " has no values: the sheet has no samples";
      asserting_null("stop");
    }
    if (length(@bad) > 0) {
      eprint @col . "_zscore: " . @col . " is missing or not a number in " . joinv(@bad, ", ");
      asserting_null("stop");
    }
    if (@min == @max) {
      eprint @col . "_zscore: " . @col . " has the same value in every sample, " . joinv(@ids, ", ");
      asserting_null("stop");
    }
    n = length(@rec); sum = 0; ss = 0;
    for (i, r in @rec) { sum += r[@col] }
    mean = sum / n;
    for (i, r in @rec) { ss += (r[@col] - mean) ** 2 }
    sd = sqrt(ss / (n - 1));
    for (i, r in @rec) { @rec[i][@col . "_zscore"] = (r[@col] - mean) / sd }
    emit > @out, @rec
  }'
detk-util record -q -i sample_info.csv -o sample_info.age_zscore.csv -- \
  mlr --icsv --ocsv put -q -s col=age -s out=sample_info.age_zscore.csv "$zscore" sample_info.csv

docs.title: Several derived columns, and the design
docs.text:
Each recipe reads one sheet and writes another, so to add several columns, run them one after another, each reading the sheet the one before wrote. Then name the derived column in the design, as any other column:

$ detk-de deseq2 -o de_results.csv "counts ~ age_zscore + condition[control]" counts.csv sample_info.age_zscore.csv

Each detk-util record wrote a module JSON document to detk_report/json/ naming the tool, mlr, and its version, with the command and the checksum of every file it read and wrote. So detk-report generate lists each recipe as a recorded step, and the provenance crate shows it as the step that produced the sheet detk-de read (see detk-util record).

docs.title: Tools overview
docs.text:
detk is organized into modules, each exposed both as a subcommand of detk and as a standalone executable (detk stats ... ≡ detk-stats ...):

Tool Purpose Needs R detk-stats count matrix statistics (distributions, zeros, entropy, PCA) no detk-filter filter features with a mini-language no detk-norm DESeq2 / library-size / FPKM normalization no detk-transform plog / rlog / VST transformations rlog, vst detk-de DESeq2 and Firth logistic differential expression yes detk-enrich fgsea pre-ranked gene set enrichment yes detk-outlier outlier count identification and shrinkage no detk-util tidy counts/column-data files against each other no detk-wrapr run custom R scripts through the detk R bridge yes detk-report render accumulated results into an HTML report no

docs.title: Common options
docs.text:
Every subcommand accepts these options in addition to its own (except detk-util record, which writes no table and so has no -d); its --help lists them under common options:. A tool's page shows each subcommand's own part of its help: the usage, the positional arguments and the options. See Stability for what help promises and exit codes for how every command exits.

common options:
  -d, --out-delim CHAR  Delimiter to use for the output file (default: ,)
  --report-dir DIR      Directory to write the HTML report and module JSON into
                        (default: ./detk_report)
  --no-report           Do not write the HTML report
  --version             Print the detk version and exit
  -v, --verbose         Make log output verbose
  -q, --quiet           Turn off all logging except warnings and errors
  --shut-up             Turn off ALL logging

Most tools write their primary output to stdout by default and accept -o FILE/--output=FILE to write to a file instead. Unless --no-report is given, each invocation also records a JSON document under <report-dir>/json/ for the report.

docs.title: de — differential expression
docs.text:
Important

The model formulas in this module use detk's formula mini-language. Read that first before writing your models.

Also remember to filter prior to differential expression — the number of genes provided for hypothesis testing affects the results. You may need to filter out genes with zero expression in all samples of interest.

Each method accepts a design formula, a counts matrix file, and a column data file. Both methods run in R via the wrapr bridge and require the corresponding R package.

docs.title: deseq2
docs.text:
Command line interface to a canonical DESeq2 analysis:

detk-de deseq2 "counts ~ AgeOfDeath + Status" raw_counts.csv column_data.csv > deseq2_results.csv

Tip

  • You can provide the whole raw counts matrix with a column data file containing only the samples you care about — detk subsets for you.
  • Add brackets with the name of the reference group to control what you are comparing against, e.g. "counts ~ Status[control]".

This is roughly equivalent to the following R:

library(DESeq2)

counts <- read.csv("raw_counts.csv", rownames=1)
design.mat <- read.csv("column_data.csv")

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
    countData = counts,
    colData = design.mat,
    design = ~ AgeOfDeath + Status
)

dds <- DESeq(dds, minReplicatesForReplace=Inf)
write.csv(results(dds, independentFiltering=FALSE, cooksCutoff=Inf), de.out.fn)

The analysis implemented here differs from the default DESeq2 analysis in the following ways:

  • the design formula must have counts as the only term on the left hand side
  • no outlier mean trimming based on Cook's distance is performed
  • no p-values or adjusted p-values are flagged or omitted due to outliers
  • estimated parameters, statistics, and p-values are reported for all variables in the model, rather than just the last term (request the DESeq2 default with --last-term-only)
  • no independent filtering is performed
  • every output column is prefixed with its model term, e.g. Status__case__log2FoldChange for the case level of Status
usage: detk-de deseq2 [options] <design> <counts_fn> <cov_fn>

positional arguments:
  <design>     Model formula, quoted, such as "counts ~ group"
  <counts_fn>  Counts file: features in rows, samples in columns, delimited

docs.title: firth
docs.text:
When comparing two classes of samples, Firth's logistic regression as described by Choi et al has desirable statistical properties: a better controlled type I error rate, and less loss of power from including additional covariates, compared with other DE methods including DESeq2. It uses a penalized likelihood to avoid complete separation of the data, a common occurrence in RNA-seq. The trade-off is that it needs more samples than negative-binomial methods — at least ~10 replicates per condition.

A counts term must be included on the right hand side of the design formula, with the sample class on the left:

detk-de firth "Status ~ AgeOfDeath + counts" norm_counts.csv column_data.csv > firth_results.csv

docs.title: enrich — set enrichment methods
docs.text: Statistical set enrichment methods, currently pre-ranked Gene Set Enrichment Analysis via the fgsea Bioconductor package (requires R).

docs.title: fgsea
docs.text:
Perform pre-ranked GSEA on a differential expression (or any) result file against a GMT gene set file.

The GMT file must be tab delimited with the set name in the first column, a description in the second (ignored by detk), and one feature ID per column after that — one feature set per line. The result file can be any character delimited file with column names in the first row.

The feature IDs must come from the same identifier system (gene symbols, ENSGIDs, ...) in both files. You will likely need to provide:

  • -i <col> — column in the results file containing feature IDs
  • -c <col> — column containing the ranking statistic, e.g. cond__treated__log2FoldChange, the log fold change of the treated level of cond, as detk-de deseq2 names it

-c is required whenever the results have more than one numeric column besides the ID column (counted after -i), as every detk-de result does: without it, detk-enrich fgsea exits 2 with a line naming the candidate columns, before R runs. A table with one numeric column besides the ID column ranks by it without -c. The module JSON records the ranking used in its params: statcol, idcol and ascending. (In 1.0.0, without -c, fgsea ranked silently by the last numeric column, which in a DESeq2 result is an adjusted p-value.)

The module JSON records the GMT as in_file_path and both inputs, the GMT and the results file, in in_file_paths, so the report's Process Run Crate lists the results file as an input of the fgsea action and links the enrichment to the step that wrote its ranking. (In 1.0.0 the results file appeared only in the recorded command line.)

detk-enrich fgsea -o gsea_results.csv -i gene -c cond__treated__log2FoldChange msigdb_c2cp.gmt deseq2_results.csv

docs.title: filter — filtering count matrices
docs.text:
Filter features (rows) out of a counts matrix using a compact filter mini-language.

usage: detk-filter [options] <command> <counts_fn> [<cov_fn>]

positional arguments:
  <command>    Filter expression: the rows to keep, quoted
  <counts_fn>  Counts file: features in rows, samples in columns, delimited
  <cov_fn>     Column data file: samples in rows, covariates in columns, for
               group filters

options:
  -h, --help         Print this help and exit
  -o, --output FILE  Name of the output file (default: stdout)

Quick start — keep only genes with a mean count greater than 10:

detk-filter -o counts_gt10.csv 'mean(all) > 10' norm_counts.csv

docs.title: The filter mini-language
docs.text:
A filter command has the form, enclosed in single or double quotes:

<function>(<column spec>) <inequality> <number>

The command describes rows that should be kept; rows not meeting the criterion are filtered out.

Available filter functions:

Function Keeps rows based on... mean the mean value across the column spec median the median value across the column spec max the maximum value across the column spec min the minimum value across the column spec zero how many counts are zero. A number strictly between 0 and 1 is interpreted as a fraction of samples; 0 or ≥ 1 as an absolute number of samples nonzero how many counts are nonzero, with the same fraction/absolute interpretation

The supported inequalities are >, >=, <, <=, ==, and !=. Numbers may be positive or negative, integer or floating point. Whitespace is ignored: mean(all)>10 ≡ mean(all) > 10.

Terms combine with and / or. and binds tighter than or, and both group to the left, as in Python, SQL and R. So

mean(all) > 5 and nonzero(all) > 0.9 or mean(all) > 100

is read as (mean(all) > 5 and nonzero(all) > 0.9) or mean(all) > 100, and a or b and c as a or (b and c). Parentheses group as written:

mean(all) > 10 and zero(all) < 0.5
(mean(all) > 5 and nonzero(all) > 0.9) or mean(all) > 100

The second example keeps lowly-but-consistently expressed rows plus any row with an overall mean above 100.

docs.title: Incorporating column data
docs.text:
Passing a column data file lets filters operate per sample group. Given column data like:

sample_name, condition
A, test
B, test
C, test
D, control
E, control

Group-wise filtering — name a column data column as the column spec, and the filter is applied to each group separately; a row is kept if any group passes:

mean(condition) > 10

keeps genes whose mean count exceeds 10 in either the test or control samples. This enables expressive schemes like:

nonzero(condition) > 0.5

which retains genes expressed in more than half the samples of either condition — genes uniquely expressed in one group survive, where filtering on the overall mean would discard them.

Group-specific filtering — subset to one level of the column:

mean(condition[test]) > 10

keeps genes whose mean exceeds 10 in the test samples, regardless of the control counts.

docs.title: norm — normalizing count matrices
docs.text: Count normalization strategies. None of these subcommands require R — the DESeq2 procedure is a Python port.

docs.title: deseq2
docs.text:
Normalize using the median-of-ratios method as implemented in the R package DESeq2: each sample is divided by a size factor calculated as the median ratio of each gene count to the geometric mean count across all samples.

usage: detk-norm deseq2 [options] <counts_fn>

positional arguments:
  <counts_fn>  Counts file: features in rows, samples in columns, delimited

options:
  -h, --help           Print this help and exit
  -o, --output FILE    Destination of normalized output in CSV format
                       (default: stdout)
  --size-factors FILE  Write out the size factors found by the DESeq2 method to
                       a two column tab separated file: a header line 'sample',
                       'size_factor', then one line per sample of its name and
                       size factor

The implementation is roughly equivalent to the following R:

library(DESeq2)

counts <- as.matrix(read.table(counts.fn, row.names=1))
colData <- data.frame(name=seq(ncol(counts)))

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
    countData=counts,
    colData=colData,
    design = ~ 1
)

dds <- estimateSizeFactors(dds)
write.table(counts(dds, normalized=TRUE), norm.counts.fn)

docs.title: library
docs.text:
Library size normalization: counts in each column are divided by the sum of that column, so each column of the output sums to 1. Use cpm for the same values scaled to counts per million.

usage: detk-norm library [options] <counts_fn>

positional arguments:
  <counts_fn>  Counts file: features in rows, samples in columns, delimited

options:
  -h, --help         Print this help and exit
  -o, --output FILE  Destination of normalized output in CSV format
                     (default: stdout)

docs.title: cpm
docs.text:
Counts Per Million: counts in each column are divided by the sum of that column and multiplied by one million, so each column of the output sums to 1,000,000. This is library scaled by 10^6.

cpm rejects a counts file that cannot be counts. It exits 1 (a bad input file), writes no output and no report, and prints one line on stderr naming the first offender, when the file has:

  • a sample named more than once in the header (gene,A,A,B), read from the header as written, before pandas would rename the second A to A.1
  • a feature ID listed more than once
  • a negative count, named by its feature, sample and value
  • a sample whose counts sum to 0 (zero depth), which has no counts per million

For example:

$ detk-norm cpm counts.csv
detk-norm: error: counts.csv: sample 'A' has no counts: its counts sum to 0 (--verbose for the traceback)

usage: detk-norm cpm [options] <counts_fn>

positional arguments:
  <counts_fn>  Counts file: features in rows, samples in columns, delimited

options:
  -h, --help         Print this help and exit
  -o, --output FILE  Destination of normalized output in CSV format
                     (default: stdout)

docs.title: fpkm
docs.text:
Fragments Per Kilobase per Million reads: each count is divided by the feature's length in kilobases, then by the sample's library size (the total of its column of counts) in millions:

FPKM[g, s] = count[g, s] / (length[g] / 1000) / (library_size[s] / 10^6)
           = count[g, s] * 10^9 / (length[g] * library_size[s])
library_size[s] = sum over g of count[g, s]

For example, a feature 2,000 bases long with 3 counts, in a sample whose counts total 4, has FPKM 3 × 10^9 / (2000 × 4) = 375,000. FPKM is CPM divided by the length in kilobases. A sample whose counts are all zero has no FPKM values: its column is empty (NaN) and a warning is logged.

Changed in 1.0

Before 1.0 (0.9.x), fpkm computed count / (10^6 × length), without dividing by library size. Values from 1.0 on differ from 0.9.x output and are the documented FPKM.

detk must be given the length of every feature in the counts file, as a two-column character-delimited file (format is sniffed) of feature identifier and length in bases:

  • every feature in the counts file must have an entry in the lengths file
  • every length must be a positive number; a zero, negative, missing or non-numeric length is refused (reported as not a positive number)
  • each feature may be listed only once; a lengths file that lists a feature twice is refused
  • the lengths file may contain unused entries
  • the two files do not need to be in the same order
  • feature identifiers are read and matched as text, exactly as written: numeric identifiers (such as Entrez gene IDs) match, a zero-padded 007 matches only 007 (not 7), and every identifier appears in the output as in the counts file
  • an optional header line is allowed: the first line is skipped as a header only when its length field is text that is neither a number nor a missing-value token (empty, NA, NaN, N/A, NULL, None); otherwise it is read as a feature
usage: detk-norm fpkm [options] <counts_fn> <lengths_fn>

positional arguments:
  <counts_fn>   Counts file: features in rows, samples in columns, delimited
  <lengths_fn>  Feature lengths file: feature name and length in bases

options:
  -h, --help         Print this help and exit
  -o, --output FILE  Destination of normalized output in CSV format
                     (default: stdout)

docs.title: tpm
docs.text:
Transcripts Per Million: each count is divided by the feature's length in kilobases, giving a per-kilobase rate, and each column of rates is then scaled to sum to 1,000,000:

rate[g, s] = count[g, s] / (length[g] / 1000)
TPM[g, s]  = rate[g, s] / sum over g of rate[g, s] * 10^6

Unlike FPKM, TPM values sum to the same total in every sample, so the proportion of a sample's transcripts a feature represents is comparable across samples. When every feature has the same length, TPM equals CPM.

tpm takes the same lengths file as fpkm, with the same rules (including the optional header line and the refusal of duplicated feature identifiers, and the requirement that every length be a positive number). The output has the same rows, in the same order, as the counts file. A sample whose counts are all zero has no TPM (or CPM) values: its column is empty (NaN) and a warning is logged.

usage: detk-norm tpm [options] <counts_fn> <lengths_fn>

positional arguments:
  <counts_fn>   Counts file: features in rows, samples in columns, delimited
  <lengths_fn>  Feature lengths file: feature name and length in bases

options:
  -h, --help         Print this help and exit
  -o, --output FILE  Destination of normalized output in CSV format
                     (default: stdout)

docs.title: outlier — outlier identification
docs.text: Functions for identifying and manipulating outlier counts.

docs.title: entropy
docs.text:
Identify samples that dominate low-entropy features. See detk-stats entropy for the underlying statistic.

usage: detk-outlier entropy [options] <counts_fn>

positional arguments:
  <counts_fn>  Counts file: features in rows, samples in columns, delimited

options:
  -h, --help          Print this help and exit
  -p, --percentile N  The entropy percentile below which a feature is flagged,
                      between 0 and 1 (default: 0.05)
  -o, --output FILE   Destination of the entropy and flag of each feature in CSV
                      format
  --plot-output FILE  Destination of a PNG plot of the entropy distribution and
                      threshold

docs.title: shrink
docs.text:
Shrink the counts of a sample that holds an outsized fraction of a feature's counts toward the feature's other samples (Labadorf et al., PLoS ONE 2015). Each feature is judged on its own, across the samples: a sample whose count is more than -p (p_max) of the feature's total is moved toward the largest count of a sample under p_max, by -f of the difference, and this repeats until no sample is over. With p_max 0.5, a feature counted 1, 1, 1, 300 becomes 1, 1, 1, 2.168; a feature with the same count in every sample is left as it is.

  • A feature whose counts are all in samples over p_max, for one a feature counted in only one sample, has no sample to shrink toward: it is written as read, and a warning gives how many features were left so (DETK-0861).
  • -p must be from 1 / number of samples to 1: below 1 / number of samples, a feature with equal counts in every sample is over it, so the command exits 2 naming the bound. When not given, p_max is sqrt(1 / number of samples).

1.0.0 compared each sample's count with that sample's total across features, not with the feature's total across samples, so its results differ for every input (see the CHANGELOG, 1.0.1).

The counts may be integers, the usual input, or decimals. The output is always decimal: a shrunk count is a fraction (an integer count of 301 may become 30.0625), so integer counts are converted to decimals first and the output is the same as for the same counts written with decimals. The Python shrink and pmf_transform functions do the same and return float counts, and raise ValueError for a p_max out of range.

usage: detk-outlier shrink [options] <counts_fn>

positional arguments:
  <counts_fn>  Counts file: features in rows, samples in columns, delimited

options:
  -h, --help             Print this help and exit
  -o, --output FILE      Destination of the shrunk counts in CSV format
                         (default: stdout)
  -f, --shrink-factor N  Shrinkage factor, between 0 and 1 (default: 0.25)
  -p, --p-max N          Largest fraction of a feature's counts one sample may
                         hold, from 1 / number of samples to 1 (when not given,
                         sqrt(1 / number of samples))
  -i, --iters N          Number of iterations (default: 1000)

docs.title: stats — count matrix statistics
docs.text:
Easy access to informative count matrix statistics. Each subcommand produces:

  • a tabular form of the statistics on stdout (or -o FILE), formatted as CSV or a human-readable table (-f table, via terminaltables)
  • a JSON document recorded under the report directory with the same statistics in machine-parsable form

docs.title: Tabular output format
docs.text:
Each tool prints CSV to standard output by default:

$ detk-stats basestats test_counts.csv
stat,val
num_cols,3
num_rows,4

Pass -f table to pretty-print instead:

$ detk-stats basestats -f table test_counts.csv
+basestats-+-----+
| stat     | val |
+----------+-----+
| num_cols | 4   |
| num_rows | 3   |
+----------+-----+

The summary subcommand runs multiple subtools; its CSV output separates each tool's table with a #<name> comment line, and its pretty-printed output prints each table serially.

docs.title: summary
docs.text:
Run the whole stats battery at once — equivalent to running basestats, coldist, colzero, rowzero, entropy, and pca separately.

usage: detk-stats summary [options] <counts_fn> [<cov_fn>]

positional arguments:
  <counts_fn>  Counts file: features in rows, samples in columns, delimited
  <cov_fn>     Column data file: samples in rows, covariates in columns

options:
  -h, --help         Print this help and exit
  --color-col COL    Column of the column data to color the output plots by
  --bins N           Number of bins of the calculated distributions
                     (default: 20)
  --log              log10 transform the counts first (zeros are left out)
  --density          Report each distribution as a density, divided by its sum
  -o, --output FILE  Destination of primary output (default: stdout)
  -f, --format FMT   Format of output (choices: csv, table) (default: csv)

docs.title: basestats
docs.text:
Basic statistics of the counts file: number of samples and number of rows.

docs.text:
Column-wise distribution of counts. Each column is binned by percentile, with output identical to that produced by np.histogram. Recorded per column: the bin boundaries, the (raw or density) mass in each bin, and extrema beyond 1.5× the inner quartile range.

  -o, --output FILE  Destination of primary output (default: stdout)
  -f, --format FMT   Format of output (choices: csv, table) (default: csv)

Row-wise analog of coldist: the distribution of counts within each feature across samples.

docs.title: colzero
docs.text:

positional arguments:

docs.text:
Number and fraction of exact-zero counts for each row (feature) — the key statistic for deciding filtering thresholds.

positional arguments:

options:

docs.title: entropy
docs.text:
Row-wise Shannon entropy of counts across samples. For each row, the fraction of the row's counts contributed by each sample is treated as a probability distribution and its entropy H = -Σ p_i · log2(p_i) computed. Rows with very low H have most of their count mass in a small number of samples — these are the rows likely to drive spurious results in downstream analysis, e.g. differential expression.

  -o, --output FILE  Destination of primary output (default: stdout)
  -f, --format FMT   Format of output (choices: csv, table) (default: csv)

detk-transform rlog norm_counts.csv > rlog_norm_counts.csv

To perform a non-blind transformation, provide a design formula and column data file:

options:

docs.title: util — counts, column data and result file utilities
docs.text: Functions for tidying up counts and column data files — mostly subsetting one or the other so the sample IDs and their order match. Combined with csvgrep from csvkit, this is useful for extracting subsets of samples for downstream differential expression analysis. gather builds the counts matrix from per-sample quantifier outputs in the first place, and annotate adds feature metadata, such as gene symbols, to a result table. record runs a command outside detk (Miller, awk, an R script) and records it as a step, so the files it writes have a producer in detk's provenance.

docs.title: gather
docs.text:
Combine per-sample outputs of salmon (quant.sf), kallisto (abundance.tsv), htseq-count or featureCounts into one counts matrix, with a row per feature and a column per sample, ready for every other detk tool.

usage: detk-util gather [options] <files>...

positional arguments:
  <files>  Quantifier output files, one per sample (a quoted glob is expanded)

options:
  -h, --help          Print this help and exit
  --format FMT        Format of the files; auto detects it from each file's
                      header (choices: salmon, kallisto, htseq, featurecounts,
                      auto) (default: auto)
  --column COL        Column to extract from each file, by name or 0-based
                      position (without it: the format's count column)
  --name-from REGEX   Regular expression deriving each sample name from its file
                      path (the first group, or the whole match)
  --on-mismatch WHAT  What to do when the samples list different features: stop
                      with an error, fill with 0 or drop them (choices: error,
                      fill, drop) (default: error)
  -o, --output FILE   Destination of the counts matrix (default: stdout)

For a salmon run per sample in sample_1__salmon/, sample_2__salmon/, ...:

detk-util gather --name-from='(sample_[0-9]+)__salmon' -o raw_counts.csv \
    sample_*__salmon/quant.sf

Formats. With --format=auto (the default) each file's format is detected from its first lines, never from its name: salmon and kallisto by their exact header line, featureCounts by its # Program:featureCounts line or its Geneid Chr Start End Strand Length header, and htseq-count by a first line with no header whose fields after the ID are integers. Every file must have the same format; a file that matches none of these is refused with a request for --format.

Columns. One column is extracted from each file, as written:

format default column other useful columns salmon NumReads TPM kallisto est_counts tpm htseq the count column (1) featurecounts every count column one BAM's column

Pick another with --column, by header name or 0-based position. htseq-count 0.13 and later, given several BAM files, writes one count column per BAM and no header naming them; such a file is refused unless --column picks one of its columns (--column=2 for the second BAM), so that no sample is lost silently. Run htseq-count once per sample to gather them all.

Feature IDs and values are kept exactly as written (9.512 stays 9.512, 007 stays 007). Every value must be a plain finite number as quantifiers write them: digits with an optional sign, decimal fraction and exponent (42, 9.512, 1.5e-06). Anything else, including NA, nan, inf, padded values and digit separators (1_000, 1,000), is an error, as is a feature listed twice in one file. htseq-count's summary lines (__no_feature, __ambiguous, ...) are not features: they are left out of the matrix and their values recorded in the report. gather does no aggregation: transcript-level salmon or kallisto output gives a transcript-level matrix.

Sample names. By default a sample is named after its file, without the last extension (s1.counts.txt becomes s1.counts). When those names are not unique among the files given, as with salmon's quant.sf and kallisto's abundance.tsv, every sample is named after the directory holding its file instead, all or nothing. A default name therefore depends on the other files in the run: a single s1/quant.sf is named quant, but s1 when gathered with s2/quant.sf. Use --name-from for names that never change. With --name-from, the name is the first group of the regular expression, or else its whole match, searched in the path as given. In featureCounts output each count column is a sample, named the same way from the column header (the BAM file's path), so bam/A.bam becomes A. Two samples with the same name are an error.

Order. The samples are written in the order of the files on the command line (featureCounts' columns in their order within the file). A quoted glob that gather expands itself is taken in natural order, comparing runs of digits as numbers, so s2 comes before s10; a glob the shell expands is in the shell's order, which is usually s1, s10, s2. detk's other tools match samples by name, so the order rarely matters.

Features. The rows follow the first sample's features. Samples quantified against the same index or annotation list the same features, so by default a difference is an error that says which samples lack how many features, with examples; it usually means a sample was quantified against another annotation. When the difference is expected, --on-mismatch=fill keeps every feature (features some samples lack are appended in order of appearance) and writes 0 where a sample lacks one, and --on-mismatch=drop keeps only the features every sample lists.

The report records the format, the column, the samples and their source files, the number of features, how many features and values were filled or dropped with examples, and htseq-count's summary lines. The input files are listed in the module's parameters (files).

docs.title: tidy
docs.text:
Subset both the counts columns and the column data rows by intersection, returning new outputs for both. The tidied column data is only written if you pass -p.

usage: detk-util tidy [options] <counts_fn> <cov_fn>

positional arguments:
  <counts_fn>  Counts file: features in rows, samples in columns, delimited

options:
  -h, --help                  Print this help and exit
  -o, --output FILE           Destination of tidied counts data
                              (default: stdout)

                              Destination of tidied column data (not written
                              without it)
